W7167102892.t: ABSTRACT: This paper explores how design fiction and generative AI (GAI) were used in a master’s course addressing food consumption issues. Data from two course iterations include student outputs, reflections, and prompt records. GAI expanded speculative exploration, supporting rich, detailed futures. Two approaches emerged, exploratory and goal-oriented, highlighting the value of prompt literacy, iteration, and critical curation to sustain creative control and adaptability.

W7167407851.t: The theme track Opening Up Design Impact Assessment: From Singular Metrics to Plural Understandings addresses the limitations of conventional approaches that rely on standardised and predominantly quantitative metrics. The ten contributions in this track therefore explore alternative ways of understanding design impact, considering it as a situated, relational, and interpretative phenomenon. Instead of proposing a single evaluative framework, the papers collectively demonstrate how impact emerges through diverse practices, contexts, and forms of knowledge. The track is organised into two complementary sessions: one that reconfigures structured approaches to assessment, and another that foregrounds lived experience and participatory processes. Together, they point toward a more plural and reflexive understanding of design impact, where evaluation becomes an ongoing process of interpretation and sensemaking rather than a fixed act of measurement.

W7167407988.t: Design continues to operate through assumptions inherited from its industrial and epistemic origins, yet the contributions gathered here unsettle those defaults and propose alternative orientations for practice. They examine how design problems are framed, how publics are organised, and how designers themselves are produced under specific historical and political conditions. Spanning urban governance, feminist methodologies, grassroots archival infrastructures, digital representation, relational approaches to AI, and critiques of universalised design expertise, the papers illuminate how counter-practices cultivate alternative publics and expand the epistemic boundaries of design. Counter Design appears not as a unified method or approach but as a constellation of refusals and propositions that expands what design can notice, value, and nourish. Collectively, these works demonstrate how design can support multiple histories and futures by challenging dominant epistemologies and opening space for alternative ways of knowing, acting, and designing.

W7167412051.t: Textiles have long nurtured philosophical positions and metaphors, inquiries, as well as investigations of making and everyday life aesthetics and processes. Performing ontologically and epistemologically at different scales, textiles are often used as case studies in interdisciplinary research. This track presents a varied selection of papers that take textiles as starting points for critical and theoretical investigations of our world, our modes of production and conditions of living, as well as their intersections. These papers focus on the way that practice, perception, usability and critical inquiry are theorized through the lens of textiles, and the way that textiles inform and support new ways of doing, learning, accessing, sensing, using and reflecting.

W7167413076.t: Guided by a deliberate undoing of design’s attachment to acceleration and forward progression, this theme track sets out to advance a practice of epistemic reuse, aiming to cultivate spaces for reflection, hesitation, and generative reuse. Returning and circling back to a previous proposition is not to be confused with trying to resurrect the past. Instead, it suggests the demand to insist on the value of remaining with unresolved tensions, feminist figurations and the complex entanglements of more-than-human worlds. The contributions to this track, in various ways, support the shift in attention from heroic innovation toward more careful, situated engagements by embracing planetary excesses and opening sensibilities towards that which exceeds us and that which cannot be fully designed.

W7167415748.t: This theme track builds on emerging research that foreground time as relational, situated, and plural, while examining how a shift towards more-than-human temporalities could reshape design practices, material engagements, and ethical responsibilities. The track proposes five areas of exploration: a) experimental representations of entangled temporalities; b) material transformations, geological formations, and temporal scales of planetary life; c) accounts on practices of noticing, attuning, and orchestrating more-than-human times; d) designerly ways of negotiating and coordinating rhythms; and e) etico-onto-epistemological reflections on time and design. The contributions engage these areas across contexts such as coastal ecologies, plant systems, and bio-based materials, framing more-than-human time as dynamic and often in tension with productivist paradigms. Collectively, they position design as a practice of temporal attunement and negotiation, fostering more reciprocal, care-driven, and ecologically grounded ways of engaging with the world.

W7167415761.t: This theme critically examines boundary objects – work arrangements, artefacts and representations facilitating cooperation across diverse social groups [1, 2] – at the intersection of sound and design. Our fundamental question is: how effectively can objects informed or defined by sound and listening fulfil this important role in design [3]? Sound-driven design [4, 5] addresses complex socio-technological challenges induced by sound to design for sonic habitability: positive auditory experiences that enhance well-being, foster social connection, and promote a more harmonious relationship between humans, their technologies, and their environments [6]. Sonic boundary objects leverage sound and listening to structure information and bridge perspectives among different communities of practices. By telling stories, enhancing performance or creating a setting, annotated sounding prototypes, experiential sound maps, audio segments or sonic sketches, semantic portraits, etc. [7, 8] contribute to transmit, preserve and receive oral know-how. They act as mediators between ill-structured ideas and specific solutions, empowering diverse groups of listeners to align understanding, cooperate and mobilise action [9, 10]. However, a critical lens is essential. How do the ephemeral and subjective qualities of sound challenge the stability required for a boundary object to have common identity? How do boundary objects shape listening instead? What methodologies effectively capture and represent sonic experiences for shared understanding without oversimplification? How do power dynamics and work arrangements influence the creation, interpretation, and use of sonic boundary objects? We encourage papers exploring practical implementations, limitations, and theoretical advancements of sonic boundary objects, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of their role in design research.

W7167416127.t: This track brings together papers that explore more-than-human design practices that generate alternative, plural, situated, and relational approaches to climate futures through affect, aesthetics, and care. Framing climate crisis as a polycrisis of interconnected ecological, political, cultural, and epistemic conditions, the track foregrounds how designers are working across contradictory, incommensurable, and unevenly recognised and experienced impacts of climate change. The included papers examine how more-than-human design can attend to embodied, felt, and sensed worlds of multiple species and digital-material entities, infrastructures, and their environments. Across landscapes, waterscapes, governance, microbial growth, and multiple intelligences, the contributions reveal both the possibilities and frictions of designing as a critical transdisciplinary practice towards more equitable, regenerative, and care-full climate futures under conditions of polycrisis.

W7167416301.t: The open track welcomes design research that explores distinctive directions beyond the conference's thematic streams, thereby enriching the scholarly discourse with diverse perspectives. The selected papers are divided into four sessions. The first session, Relational and Situated Design Practice, foregrounds embodiment, exchange, co-exploration, ritual performance, feminist critique, and cultural remembrance. The second session, Material, Mind and Machine, investigates the entanglements among physical matter, human cognition, and computational processes, challenging the separation among the object, the mind, and the machine that mediates them. The third session, Strategic Design Practices for Learning, Attention, and Co-Creation, discusses strategic design, together with means of engaging with complex problems in contemporary organizations and across different fields, and the fourth session, Human Experience in Product and Interface Design, brings together empirical studies across product design, interface and interaction design and studies that deal with customer reaction to advertising strategies and customer decision-making journeys.

W7167422802.t: Design research involving practice affords a unique mode of inquiry facilitated by acts of making, generative thinking, and iterative experimentation. The practitioner’s perspective is central because it foregrounds the significance of personal engagement with the research problem at hand. Current efforts in the field are nonetheless aiming to expand this inward-looking gaze by attending to the systemic and entangled dimensions of designing. With the increasing turn to relational, posthuman, and decolonial approaches towards that end, it becomes imperative to reconstrue what counts as ‘practice’ and reexamine whose perspectives are included in such a reconstrual. The present track brings together five contributions dealing with this issue, offering an array of theoretical, empirical, and methodological studies that illustrate how design research involving practice can fully account for the centrality of the practitioner’s perspective while also addressing the urgency to decenter it.

W7167423539.t: Grounded in post-anthropocentric and post-humanist perspectives, this track explores more-than-human data practices that challenge dominant data paradigms and cultivate alternative modes of engagement with the world, from the microbial to the planetary. Rather than treating non-human life as objects of measurement and classification, as data subjects, the contributions in this track ask what it would mean to recognize organisms, systems, and processes as data co-producers, whose perceptual worlds, temporal rhythms, and relational entanglements actively participate in what counts as knowledge. This reorientation carries profound consequences for the designer. Co-producing data with more-than-human others is a political, epistemic, and ontological commitment that goes beyond inclusivity: it unsettles human authority, disrupts extractive infrastructures, and demands new forms of response-ability in how knowledge is gathered, represented, and put to use. If data has long spoken for the world, this track asks: how might it begin to listen?

W7167424754.t: To design for play is to engage with materials, whether physical, virtual, symbolic, or ephemeral. In design for play we don’t just select materials; we shape and are shaped by them. Yet within design research, we must explore how materials do play, not merely support it. This theme track invites contributions that consider materials not as passive tools, but as active collaborators in a relational field where matter, mood, meaning, affect, and politics entangle. We are interested in how materials act not only as substrates for play, but as collaborators, provocateurs, and agents in the making of play, relationships, and worlds. From the engineered to the ephemeral, the bodily to the speculative, how do materials provoke, resist, or shape play experiences? How might they open up new modes of care, speculation, or disruption? We welcome research that moves beyond anthropocentric or utilitarian notions of materiality for play. We are curious how play materials carry symbolic weight, generate affective charge, and invite sensorial or aesthetic encounters. This track invites both theoretical and practice-led research that challenges anthropocentric, functionalist, or engineering-driven views of materials. We encourage work open to radical critique and poetic inquiry, foregrounding entanglement, friction, and emergence over tidy categories. We particularly welcome perspectives from the margins of play design working across speculative design, activism, pedagogy, or adjacent fields, where materials become a site of inquiry and invention. What happens when we treat materials not only as designed for play, but as active in the crafting of different futures of play?

W7167903436.t: This article investigates how historical darning samplers from the textile collection of the National Museum of Denmark (NMD) can be engaged as objects of inquiry in a contemporary context in a workshop series under the NMD event format Hands in History conducted in 2024. The study highlights how textile repair and mending techniques have gained increased attention due to a growing awareness of the climate and environmental impact associated with the production, use and disposal of textile products – but also how the decline in textile knowledge and skills for undertaking mending and repairs represents a barrier for building up textile literacy. The study is based on 59 darning samplers in the NMD’s collection dating from 1721 to 1891 that tell an important story of handicraft education in Denmark, the pervasive role of textile crafts in the society of the time, and the strong ideals of this period in time associated with textile techniques. The Hands in History: Darning workshops consisted of hands-on darning exercises and lectures highlighting the history of darning samplers and how associated historical insights relate to contemporary perspectives and ongoing debates about sustainability and circularity of textiles. This article focuses on the insights obtained during the interaction between the workshop facilitator – researcher, the participants and the darning samplers in regard to historical research conducted at museums and wider contemporary perspectives on textile crafts.

W7168265132.t: Designers typically collaborate across different disciplines. We wanted to explore what it has meant to work as designers in a project situated in healthcare. Our work is part of a four-year interdisciplinary project on adolescent oral health in Norway, where we worked with dental professionals, researchers, industry partners, a youth-focused non-profit organisation, and young people to support adolescents’ oral health habits. From four cases, we reflect on three themes: connecting with ourselves as designers in a new field, connecting with the field and participants, and connecting with partners across disciplines. Entering the dental health field meant learning new technical language and clinical routines while maintaining our own way of working. Recruiting adolescents, parents, and health professionals for co-design was challenging, and we learned that co-design can happen not only in workshops but through everyday conversations and youth arenas. Change ran in both directions: as we learned to work with the structured, evidence-based traditions of dental health, our partners took on iterative ways of working common in design - a mutual change that captures interdisciplinary collaboration realistically. From a single project in a Norwegian context, findings may not transfer directly elsewhere, but may help other teams working across design and health.

W7169835608.t: The article first provides a comprehensive walkthrough of theories and perspectives we found relevant to the teaching of systemic design. As educators and practitioners, we have developed an approach to practice research in developing educational models for teaching and learning systemic design and systems-oriented design. Our experience is years of teaching at the undergraduate and graduate levels at the Oslo School of Architecture and Design. This article is Part I of II; here, we relate our praxis to existing pedagogical concepts and present our approach. The second part continues with classroom praxis and reflexive facilitation, going into details of how we teach. Some of our ways of thinking and acting are similar to concepts discussed in design education and pedagogical teaching methods. Others are more unique; at least, in some cases, it was difficult to find publications that reflect our thoughts. We think of teaching systems-oriented design as a system of different interplaying elements. It is highly dependent on the context and the abilities and personalities of the involved teachers and learners. Hence, our approach to learning in complexity respects the uniqueness of each learning situation as an enactment of an evolving social system. The combination of tools, ways of thinking and acting, and concepts flows into a flexible, adaptive ecology. It is brought together in a systemic design approach to learning situations, which can be adapted, changed, and moulded into something useful for others. We think of the student–teacher relations as complex social systems, with each holding their own motives and learning mechanisms. We look at the classroom as a system, and our role is to be part of it. This challenges the role of the teacher and student. What stands out in this approach is the assemblage of concepts, approaches and practices into an ecology of learning, a complex system in its own right.

W7170141565.t: With the rise of online retailing, consumers increasingly make purchase decisions based on small, thumbnail-sized product images, often displayed in grid formats. This shift introduces new challenges for packaging design, particularly for fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG), because size, shape, and material of the packaging—physical cues that in-store consumers use to quickly identify the products they seek—are indiscernible in online stores. This paper offers five guidelines for designing graphic elements of packaging made for display in online marketplaces. The guidelines derive from interviews with five professional packaging designers (study 1) and subsequently tested with eye-tracking in a laboratory environment (study 2). Patterns of eye movements from 61 respondents revealed that packaging designed according to the five guidelines drew significantly more visual attention and had higher customer interactions. Implementation and implication for professional designers is debated in a final section together with needs for further research.

W7171853635.t: Abstract Contemporary design operates within conditions of ecological destabilization and distributed technological agency that challenge anthropocentric and instrumental paradigms. While participatory, regenerative and AI-mediated design approaches have expanded disciplinary scope, their integration remains conceptually fragmented. This paper introduces Co-nature’ing as a positioning framework that reconceptualizes design as a metabolic epistemology – a relational mode of knowing and acting across Human–Nature–Intelligence ecologies. Grounded in process philosophy, complexity theory, ecological cognition and autopoietic systems theory, the framework advances a symmetrical triad in which biological systems and algorithmic infrastructures function as co-agents rather than resources or tools. The Co-nature’ing spiral – Co-Sensing, Co-Growing, Co-Evolving and Co-Flourishing – is presented as an operative translation of this epistemological shift. A pedagogical instantiation through the BIP Design Roadmap illustrates how distributed agency can be enacted within studio practice. The paper contributes a unified theoretical foundation for biodesign as cognitive ecology and relational co-evolution.

W7171921805.t: Public participation has long occupied a central position within planning and design theory. From Arnstein’s seminal work on citizen participation to collaborative planning, co-production, and contemporary participatory design approaches, scholars and practitioners have increasingly recognized the importance of involving citizens and users in shaping urban environments. Despite these advances, participation continues to be understood predominantly as an episodic and project-based activity associated with specific interventions, workshops, or consultation processes. Relatively limited attention has been devoted to the temporal dimensions of participation and to how users, places, meanings, and needs evolve over time. This study argues that time remains one of the least-explored dimensions of participatory planning and design. Building on literature from planning theory, participatory design, commons scholarship, care studies, and emerging work on temporality, the study proposes participatory temporal urbanism as a conceptual framework for understanding participation as an ongoing and evolving relationship rather than as a discrete event. The framework introduces five interrelated dimensions: co-creation, deliberation, co-management, co-adaptation, and co-memory. Drawing on concepts such as stewardship, commoning, maintenance, and care, the study further argues that sustainable urban development requires forms of participation that extend beyond implementation and continue throughout the life cycle of places. Particular attention is given to deliberative approaches, including the jury principle associated with New Urbanism, and to the role of participatory design in accommodating changing social, cultural, and intergenerational needs. By introducing time as a central analytical category, the study contributes to ongoing debates on participatory planning and participatory design and offers a new framework for understanding the collective processes through which sustainable cities can be collectively shaped, maintained, and continuously reinterpreted over time.

W7172454570.t: This study maps the academic literature produced between 2000 and 2025 in the field of ludic architecture through bibliometric methods, revealing the transformation of play from a marginal tool into an ontological actor within architectural discourse. A total of 268 publications retrieved from the Web of Science database were analyzed using VOSviewer, through which temporal trends, geographical distributions, disciplinary relations, co-authorship networks, and conceptual clusters were identified. The findings demonstrate that ludic architecture has evolved into an increasingly institutionalized, multilayered, and interdisciplinary research domain shaped by digital technologies, participatory practices, and post-anthropocentric ontologies. By clarifying how ludic agency has become an epistemic framework in architectural knowledge production, pedagogical approaches, and spatial practices, the study offers the first comprehensive bibliometric mapping of the field.

W7202095742.t: Service design has broadened its aims from new service development towards service system transformation. Despite the complexity, uncertainty and non-linearity of such an ambition, service design continues to employ project-based structures to organize its processes. Recognizing that such organizing frameworks often limit service design’s transformative potential, this paper explores how a programmatic approach can be applied to service design practice aimed at service system transformation. Drawing on learnings from three service design programs conducted in Norway and Sweden, we outline four core contributions of a programmatic approach to service system transformation: 1) supporting open-ended inquiry; 2) encouraging situated experimentation; 3) promoting adaptation through oscillation; and 4) cultivating collective reflexive action. This paper unpacks the struggles that adopting a programmatic approach in practice entails and offers practical considerations for practitioners in how to steward a programmatic approach.

W7202198639.t: Modern IT systems often fail to adequately support users’ everyday work, negatively affecting both performance and well-being. A key reason is that system development typically focuses on one system rather than considering how users interact with multiple systems at work. This paper argues that digitalisation efforts must move beyond traditional, system-bounded design to explicitly address the whole digital work environment. This synthesis study examines three design methods aimed at improving understanding of digital work environments: Contextual Personas and Contextual Think-Aloud, applied in student software projects, and the Vision Seminars method, used in a large-scale, realistic software project. All three methods seek to help IT professionals gain deeper insights into how users work across multiple systems. A qualitative meta-analysis study of six empirical studies is conducted, assessing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of each design method. The findings indicate that the design methods support a better understanding of users’ digital work environments, incorporating not only technical aspects but also well-being and psychological and social dimensions. Identified weaknesses involve risks of stereotyping, challenges for some users during evaluation, and high resource demands. Overall, the paper concludes that designing systems aligned with real digital work environments is both necessary and achievable.

W7202378516.t: This introduction to the Transparent Autonomy and Human Work Interaction Design workshop presents the workshop’s topic, its motivations, and the papers published on the proposed research theme. This workshop was collocated with the INTERACT2025 conference in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. The workshop proposed investigating the design of autonomous systems’ transparency with the aim of enabling effective and pleasant collaboration with these systems at work. From the initial workshop papers, this volume presents extended and novel propositions to contribute to human work interaction design of autonomy transparency.

W7203581634.t: Introduction: Human-drone interaction is an emerging field investigating ways to extend the conventionally passive role of drones with autonomous, socially interactive functionalities. Drones offer unique opportunities for applications, such as exercise support, due to their mobility and flexibility. While previous research has studied drones for, e.g., pacing, gait analysis, and accessibility in running contexts, we propose that an equally crucial part of such applications is the socially interactive role of the drone. Methods: We present a study in two phases. In the first phase, we conducted a preliminary study that informed the design of a co-design workshop through eight semi-structured interviews exploring drone support for runners. In the second phase, we designed and conducted a co-design workshop with five experienced recreational runners to reflect on the practical and ethical challenges of using drones and to envision ways in which drones could support and interact with runners in future scenarios. The collected materials were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and annotated visual analysis. Results: The results present five low-fidelity social drone prototypes, including participants' reflections tied to each prototype. Furthermore, we present analytical themes that demonstrate the necessity of extending and re-framing approaches to designing social drones. Discussion: The paper makes three key contributions. First, we offer an approach to co-designing social drones that focus on eliciting the experiences of participants and manifesting those in concrete, embodied design concepts. Second, we validate the existing Design Space for Social Drones framework through a concrete application domain. Our validation shows that the dimensions can be further detailed, and that non-user perspectives are a potentially crucial extension. Third, we present three recommendations that encapsulate concerns for further designs of social drones.

W7203923316.t: Digital simulation tools for environmental performance analysis are widely employed in architectural practices around the world. For this reason, teaching students how to use those tools is increasingly becoming an important part of the architect’s education and future employability. However, in architectural design, digital tools, providing fixed numerical outputs, have the potential to lead to design fixations, limiting the students’ capacity for innovative thinking by restricting their design actions. This study suggests that digital tools can be used not only as tools for complex computational analysis in the architect’s practice but also as pedagogical tools facilitating the integration of numerical simulation outputs in holistic design processes, enhancing the learner’s experience. The study further infers that one method to accomplish this is by incorporating digital tools into hands-on activities and experiments. To test the hypothesis, we designed and tested an experimental workshop. Action research was chosen as a methodology, enabling the researchers to participate in ongoing situations, influencing the events while simultaneously being able to measure the impact of their interventions. All activities followed Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory and Schenck & Cruickshank’s Co-constructed Developmental Teaching Theory. A set of digital and analog tools for simulating environmental performance was incorporated into the teaching and learning activities of the workshop. The juxtaposition of the different simulation capabilities of those tools aimed to provoke students to reflect and build a holistic understanding of the subtleties of simulation results. This article is the conclusion of the first workshop and summarizes the attempt to incorporate those tools into hands-on activities and experiments, encouraging students to test the boundaries of their design solutions on both quantitative and qualitative basis. The main discussion points are the methodology and methods employed in the first workshop and the agenda for improving the protocols for the next planned workshop.

W7204271466.t: Starting with a seemingly bounded design brief—studying and designing social drones—this thesis gradually opens into an inquiry into how design knowledge forms those who practice it. Rather than treating design as a neutral means of intervention, the work attends to design sensibilities: the embodied, relational orientations through which designers come to perceive, act, and live in the world. These sensibilities operateas corporeal theories; becoming a skin that accumulates, hardens, softens, and is shed over time.Theory is often treated as something we apply to practice, or extract from it after the fact. Here, there is a different premise: that theory within design is already being made in the fostering of sensibilities. I argue that attending to and articulating sensibilities as a form of intermediate-level knowledge allows us to understand it not only as abstraction, but as something that transforms bodies, relationships, and ways of being in practice. Through first-person methods, longitudinal autoethnography, and material making, the work traces a shift from naïve engagement to critical disillusionment, and onward to a reconfiguration of what it might mean to practice and theorise design otherwise. As the research moves with its time—through intensifying technological concentration exemplified by the case of drones—it bears witness to where imagination feels institutionally and intentionally foreclosed. Rather than smoothing over these ruptures, the thesis centres them as sites where design theory is remade through corporeality rather than represented as a lens. The dissertation is a non-linear constellation of collaborative experiments, including pictorials, critiques, and co-authored texts and designs structured in three chapters. The first focuses on refusing the inevitability of drones, the second describes design epistemology as sensibilities, and the third opens paths forward for design as an implication from a turn to sensibilities. This compositional choice resists the primacy of individual authorship and challenges academic norms that locate rigour in separation between theory and practice, researcher and subject, or singular voice and collective inquiry. I discuss co-constructed relational knowing not only through artefacts or arguments and shared attentiveness through reflexive and diffractive thinking and making. At its core, this thesis argues for an expanded understanding of designerly knowledge: one that takes seriously how design epistemologies act upon designers themselves. It joins conversations on design otherwise and on making trouble, proposing that withdrawal, instigation, refusal, and pauses in making are not endpoints but part of a broader repertoire of design actions in grave need of a collective stance. Design practice unfolds alongside social, political, and ecological rupture, coming to terms with its impossibility under the violence of capitalism. By articulating sensibilities as both knowledge outcome and method, the thesis invites a rethinking of design research as a practice of becoming: with others, attuned to the collective sensibilities required to navigate worlds that are increasingly difficult to design within. It culminates in a call for design as a pre-revolutionary act.

W7204438282.t: This study investigates sustainable employment within Malaysia’s creative sector by examining self-employed designers managing independent practice. As firm-based opportunities decline and freelance careers become more prevalent, the sustainability of creative work increasingly hinges on designers’ ability to navigate managerial, ethical, and relational challenges independently. The study is positioned within the gap between design education, project-based creative work, and the realities of self-managed professional practice. Using a qualitative focus group method, data were collected from six experienced entrepreneurial designers operating in sectors such as education, creative and digital media, and community-based design. Participants were purposively selected based on their experience in independent creative practice, client-based projects, nonprofit or community-orientated work, and self-employed decision-making roles. Thematic analysis followed a traceable process in which participant quotations were linked to initial codes, broader themes, and descriptive claims. A thematic analysis revealed four critical dimensions of self-employed sustainability: strategic project management, client communication, ethical design practice, and self-sustaining professional strategies. The findings describe how participants managed time, cost, resources, client expectations, ethical choices, peer support, visibility, and work–life boundaries in the absence of formal organizational support. The study integrates the Project Management Triangle and Design Management Staircase to frame these findings, using these models as frameworks for understanding the managerial and developmental capacities involved in independent design practice. The study contributes a descriptive, evidence-linked account of how experienced Malaysian self-employed designers sustain independent practice through managerial, relational, ethical, and self-governing strategies. The results underscore the disparity between conventional design education and the actual experiences of independent practitioners, where soft skills, ethical orientation, and emotional resilience are essential. Broader implications for design education and policy support are reserved for the Discussion.

W7204461629.t: The (Blinded for review) Department of Design explores innovative educational methods to support student creativity in higher education and to position the university as an incubator of innovation. One track in this endeavour is to engage students in shaping their own learning environments, thereby opening discussions on modernizing design pedagogy and fostering a culture of empowerment and innovation. As part of this ambition, we tested a novel approach in the course (Blinded for review) Design in wood (autumn 2025): “Fill the Gap: Design and Build Furniture/Furnistructures for the ID Building.” While our department is restructuring all areas, we saw an opportunity to involve design students in literally shaping their own – and future design students’ – physical environment. Working in groups, students identified and analysed leftover spaces in the Design building and proposed furniture/structures to transform them into useful places, based on the departments current and future needs, with the aim of enhancing the use of circulation areas. We interviewed students from all groups to address two research questions: (1) What is the value of involving students in co-designing their joint environment? (2) How may such co-design exercises contribute to modernizing design pedagogy and fostering a culture of empowerment and innovation in education? Our findings indicate that the exercise strengthened students’ sense of ownership, responsibility, and innovation. We argue that such co-design assignments offer significant potential for making universities incubators of empowerment and innovation, and represent a promising path for modernizing design pedagogy.

W7204470743.t: This paper presents a comparative educational case study examining how two differently framed design education projects contributed to student learning and innovation-oriented outcomes within the context of sustainable agricultural technology. The study compares two parallel university courses conducted in the UK and Sweden in collaboration with the agricultural technology company DeLaval. Rather than claiming broad pedagogical generalisations, the paper focuses specifically on how differences in project structure, technological framing, user access, and collaboration influenced student learning processes and design outcomes. The first case involved 11 individual projects completed by Advanced Design Management students at Aston University, where students developed user-centred product–service concepts informed by field visits, interviews, and market analysis. The second case involved five engineering design students at Mälardalen University who developed a virtual reality (VR) assembly-training prototype for the DeLaval VMS V300 milking robot. A cross-case qualitative analysis was conducted using design thinking framework dimensions including scope definition, degree of user engagement, working structure, contextual familiarity, and iteration practices. Findings indicate that open-ended projects encouraged broader conceptual exploration but created challenges in contextual understanding, while technology-constrained projects supported technical depth but limited conceptual diversity. Across both cohorts, limited access to users and unfamiliarity with agricultural contexts affected iteration quality and confidence in decision-making. The findings support a more cautious conclusion that international thematic alignment can enrich reflection and expose students to complementary design approaches when supported through structured interaction and contextual access. The study contributes practical insights for educators designing cross-institutional sustainability-focused design projects.

W7204474984.t: Inclusive design in apparel requires not only designing for diverse bodies but also designing with an understanding of the lived experiences, preferences, and embodied variations of users. Yet current engineering and design education continues to rely on standardized body data and idealized sizing models, leaving significant user groups unrepresented. This lack of representation contributes to design exclusion, high return rates, and unnecessary waste. As the fashion sector faces growing pressure to become more inclusive and sustainable, design education must evolve to better prepare future designers for this complexity. This paper examines how case-based learning and data-driven design processes can strengthen inclusive product development. Students are presented with authentic real-world cases consisting of qualitative interviews with women describing their experiences with clothing, fit, and style, paired with quantitative 3D body-scanning data that visually and spatially represents their embodied form. By working with this combined material, students engage directly with bodily variation and user narratives, enabling them to apply their professional knowledge more critically and contextually. The findings suggest that when diversity is embedded in both the design process and the learning environment, students develop deeper empathy, enhanced analytical reasoning, and stronger problem-framing skills. The paper proposes a model in which fit is reframed not as a narrow technical constraint but as an embodied design challenge essential to product performance. The paper contributes a pedagogical framework that brings together diversity awareness, data-driven insight, and cross-disciplinary collaboration. It highlights inclusive collection strategies that replace single systems with micro-systems designed to accommodate user variation.

W7204904413.t: This cross-national study investigates how creative thinking is manifested through design-based learning (DBL) in Singapore, Finland, and Hungary. Moving beyond the standardized metrics of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 assessment, this research utilizes a practice-based lens to examine the specific pedagogical mechanisms—problem framing, materialization, iteration, and social context—that structure everyday classroom activity. The analysis reveals that creative thinking is not a static individual trait but a situated practice profoundly shaped by institutional conditions and the degree of curricular embedding. By analyzing diverse educational settings, the study identifies how different instructional architectures prioritize specific dimensions of the creative process, from initial brainstorming to technical realization. The findings show that creative thinking does not develop evenly across domains simply through exposure to open-ended tasks. Instead, creative engagement becomes patterned through repeated participation in particular forms of design practice. Where design processes are explicitly taught and systematically reinforced, students are better able to sustain evaluation and refinement; where design activity is exploratory but weakly scaffolded, creative thinking tends to remain concentrated in ideation and expressive exploration. By bridging large-scale assessment frameworks with local classroom realities, this article argues that creative profiles are pedagogical products rather than inherent student attributes. The study suggests that fostering advanced creative competencies requires moving beyond generic “openness” toward structured, domain-sensitive instruction that legitimizes and supports iterative improvement alongside initial idea generation.

W7204993290.t: This article examines how a material-driven design approach using the snow glass technique shapes design processes and outcomes within Arctic product design. Focusing on Arctic glass design, the study explores how snow, as a locally available and temporary natural material, can be integrated into multiple stages of glass design and making processes. The research combines student perspectives on Arctic product design, collaborative practice-based experimentation with Arctic glass design, and experienced practitioners’ insights concerning the snow glass technique. The findings indicate that snow functions not only as a reference to Arctic environments but also as a processual element influencing material behaviour, form development, and surface qualities. The study identifies the distinctive characteristics of the snow glass technique and contributes to discussions on material-driven and context-sensitive approaches within Arctic glass design practices.

W7211884715.t: This paper examines how external conditions are associated with different configurations of design function organization in companies. Building on design management, silent design, design innovation ecosystems, and economic complexity, it proposes a multidimensional framework distinguishing four configurations: Hidden Design, Silent Design, Internal Design, and External Design. Using survey data from 324 companies in Chile’s Biobío Region, combined with administrative company-level records and municipality-level indicators, the study estimated binomial and multinomial logistic regression models across recognition, professionalization, and location of expertise. The results show a differentiated pattern. Local design ecosystems are closely associated with the recognition of non-professional design and professionalization of design activities, whereas sectoral R&D intensity is strongly associated with the internalization of professional design expertise. Municipal economic complexity is associated specifically with External Design, while evidence for complexity indicators remains limited and non-uniform. The study contributes a framework for analysing how design becomes visible, professionalized, and organizationally embedded.

W7211942158.t: This study explores how international and domestic students interact in a university craft course. Earlier research has shown that interaction between international and domestic students is often limited, while studies in craft education highlight craft as a communicative subject. The present study connected these fields by examining (1) how international students interact with domestic students and (2) what observable factors influence or trigger their interaction. The analysis was based on observations of video recordings from a craft course. The findings indicate that students engage with each other on their craft projects, tools, techniques, materials, personal aspects and language and cultural topics. A key factor initiating interaction is the presence of a physical craft project, which provides a shared focus that encourages communication.

W7213531788.t: Developing scaling strategies for citizens’ assemblies requires situated knowledges. Local governments are increasingly using service design methods to foreground situated knowledges; however, the design research community calls for greater reflection on their application to enable ethical learning and transformation. In contrast to reflection, the feminist metaphor of diffraction enables greater relationality, complexity, and impact within research; yet it remains a novel approach. This paper presents an experiment conducted with participants of a city-level citizens’ assembly in Sweden. During the experiment, journey mapping was used within a diffraction apparatus, incorporating diffractive reading to enable the collective exploration of barriers to and opportunities for scaling citizens’ assemblies. A diffractive approach to journey mapping shifted the researcher’s position, increasing participants’ power. Furthermore, the resulting journey map visualised plurality and complexity. More research is recommended to explore the impacts of a research methodology that combines feminist onto-epistemologies, such as diffraction, with service design methods.

W7213548648.t: The work discussed in this article aims to present and reflect upon different levels of participatory design methods applied in indoor and outdoor lighting research projects. Papers selected through a systematic literature review covering the period from 2019 to 2024 were categorized by the level of participation and corresponding research stage. The four defined stages include: locating and defining issues or problems, collecting research data, interpreting research data, and reporting research findings. The theoretical framework suggested by Kaulio (1998) was adapted to categorize the studies. The framework distinguishes three levels of participant involvement: research for (no direct participant involvement), research with (active collaboration), and research by (participant-led collaboration). Results indicate that participatory design methods are most frequently employed during the data collection stage, whereas the initial and final stages of research typically remain researcher-led. This suggests that collaboration is valued but primarily concentrated in the middle phases of research. Greater integration of participatory methods in early and late stages could improve communication of research goals and outcomes to broader audiences. These findings provide a foundation/motivation for integrating participatory methods more holistically in lighting research, strengthening user participation and context-relevant proposals.

W7213573535.t: This paper proposes a Design Culture Studies contribution to the evaluation of design impact. The existing methods of evaluating design impact predominantly focus on economic and quantitative metrics, which fail to capture the many ways, according to diverse groups, in which design can and should shape the world. As a humanities field employing interdisciplinary qualitative methods, Design Culture Studies is well positioned to respond to this challenge. To clarify the needs and opportunities for more inclusive evaluation approaches, we conducted a cross-national needs analysis combining literature review and empirical research with students, graduates, educators, design organisations, industry stakeholders, and policymakers. The analysis identified five critical requirements for inclusive evaluations of the socio-cultural impacts of design: inclusivity and diversity, rigour, practical guidelines, educational tools, and the integration of digital tools. Drawing on these insights, in this paper we propose a Design Culture Studies-led conceptual framework for pluralising the evaluation of the socio-cultural impacts of design, with an emphasis on the context of design education, on students and graduates. We argue that such a framework can foster more reflexive forms of evaluation by acknowledging how assessing design impact also participates in shaping the meanings, values, possibilities – and futures of design cultures.

W7213652146.t: Despite its ambitions to transform service systems, service design has been critiqued for reproducing the status quo and normalizing others into dominant social expectations. To move away from the circulation of hegemonic structures, the service design discipline needs to be challenged. Drawing on queer theory, this paper explores how service design can be undisciplined to create a grammar of possibility for making service systems otherwise. Based on experiences from an experimental seven-week service design research and education collaboration with hospital-based mental health services in Norway, this research presents a queer framework that highlights the failings that ensue when we play with, or dis/order, traditional service design. This research offers an opening for expansive ways of untraining, undoing and forgetting that attempt to resist mastery in service design. To encourage continued experimentation, the paper provides playful and provocative prompts for undisciplining service design in practice, education and research.

W7214568171.t: Participation in cultural life can strengthen wellbeing, social connection, and sense of purpose. However, access to cultural volunteering opportunities is often unevenly distributed, shaped by informal networks, implicit norms, and unspoken expectations about who belongs.This paper investigates how inclusive design approaches can lower participation thresholds and broaden engagement in cultural volunteering by intentionally addressing fundamental psychological needs. The study is situated within a two-year research-through-design collaboration between regional cultural institutions and a design research environment in Southern Denmark. Through ethnographic observations, interviews, stakeholder dialogues, and co-creation workshops with both active volunteers and individuals not previously engaged in cultural communities, the project identified structural and perceptual barriers to participation. These included high entry thresholds, limited visibility of opportunities, inherited volunteering cultures, perceived cultural elitism, and restricted influence in decision-making processes. Together, these factors shaped those who felt entitled, confident, and welcomed to participate. Guided by principles from inclusive design and Positive Design theory by Desmet and Pohlmeyer (2013), the project operationalised five fundamental psychological needs such as autonomy, community, competence, impact, and recognition as generative design parameters. Rather than framing inclusion solely as demographic representation, the research approached inclusion as the creation of material and organisational conditions that enable diverse forms of participation, expression, and contribution. Two interventions were developed and prototyped in situ across multiple communities: Food+Culture events and Cultural Pop-up Communities. Both formats function as low-threshold, mobile, and socially oriented entry points. By combining shared meals, creative activities, and temporary outreach in educational and public settings, the interventions reposition volunteering from a performance-based and potentially exclusionary domain toward a relational and participatory practice. The prototypes were iteratively refined through participant feedback and stakeholder reflection. Findings indicate that inclusive participation is shaped less by the intrinsic nature of cultural activities and more by how access, responsibility, and legitimacy are designed. When participation structures explicitly support autonomy, visible contribution, shared ownership, and recognition, cultural volunteering becomes more accessible and meaningful to a broader range of participants. Wellbeing emerges as a relational condition produced through designed interactions rather than as an individual outcome alone.

W7214609183.t: Maintaining situational awareness (SA) is critical for safe and effective interaction in complex environments where operators work near heavy machinery. SA is challenged by constrained spaces, limited visibility, high noise, and increasing automation, which can reduce operators’ understanding of machine behavior. Using a five-phase Research through Design approach grounded in Human-Centered Design, we investigated how human augmentation technologies (HATs) can support SA, safety, and operator–machine interaction in underground mining. Through field observations, a focus group interview, design artifacts, a co-design workshop, low-fidelity prototypes, and a validation workshop, we identified the importance of communicating machine operational state and motion intent during maintenance, testing, and troubleshooting tasks. We co-designed redundant multimodal wearable concepts and derived design guidelines for context-aware wearable HATs that support safe operator–machine interaction through anticipatory visual, auditory, and haptic feedback.

W7214634492.t: Even though standards and legislation exist to improve digital accessibility, their implementation depends on how accessibility is negotiated within everyday design practice. This study was conducted in Sweden in spring 2024, before the European Accessibility Act (EAA) became applicable, to investigate how UX/UI designers incorporated accessibility into their work and perceived forthcoming legal requirements. We conducted 11 semi-structured interviews with UX/UI designers and subsequently consulted two accessibility experts in two asynchronous rounds to evaluate and complement the interview-derived themes. Our findings show that designers frequently take on an informal accessibility advocacy and brokerage role: they educate colleagues and clients, translate accessibility requirements into design practice, seek external expertise, and repeatedly keep accessibility on the project agenda. However, they often lack authority over the budgets, timelines, staffing, and organizational priorities that determine whether accessibility is implemented. We conceptualize this tension as a responsibility–authority gap and show how it is produced through interactions between individual practice, organizational conditions, education, standards, and legislation. Based on these findings, we present empirically informed recommendations at micro, meso, and macro levels.

W7214645590.t: Managing autonomous swarms presents significant cognitive challenges, as current entity-centric interfaces fail to scale with increasing agent numbers. This paper addresses this gap by distilling intermediate-level design knowledge from Real-Time Strategy (RTS) games, which provide a rich source of precedents for multi-agent coordination. Through a generative precedent analysis of three RTS titles compared against a professional baseline swarm interface (QGroundControl), we derive six inspirational patterns for Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI). These patterns capture recurring interaction structures that may help address conflicting design forces, such as the tension between local precision and global situational awareness. Our contribution is positioned as exploratory, hypothesis-generating design research that provides a generative repertoire of design ideas aligned with the Human-Centered AI (HCAI) goal of high human control over high automation. By bridging the gap between the analysis of precedents and professional Ground Control Station (GCS) design, these patterns offer an initial basis for a design language for scalable and flexible swarm command.

W7214652794.t: User involvement is central to Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), yet enabling meaningful participation in practice requires competencies that extend beyond applying methods. This paper examines how such competencies emerge by focusing on novices learning to facilitate Participatory Design (PD) activities. We report on a qualitative study of master’s students facilitating PD activities in a university course, drawing on facilitation plans, video recordings, group interviews, and class discussions. An inductive thematic analysis identifies six recurring challenges: (1) Working with structure while adapting to unfolding situations, (2) When (not) to intervene, (3) Calibrating explanations, (4) Managing power dynamics in participation and outcomes, (5) Managing perceptions of the facilitator, and (6) Planning the PD activity and handling unexpected outcomes. By comparing these findings with prior studies of experienced facilitators, we highlight key differences in how facilitation is understood and enacted. The study contributes empirical insight into the early development of facilitation competence in PD.

W7214668154.t: In today's digitalized societies, many everyday activities are supported by digital technologies, forcing everybody to become technology users. Involuntary non-users of such normalized digital technologies experience being disabled and excluded from activities and social arenas that require use of digital technologies that they are unable to use. In this paper, we argue that our understanding of non-use in the digitalized society needs to be widened with discussions about forced use, as this is a basis for making non-use problematic. Building on Participatory Design (PD), our second aim is to show how and why PD is an effective approach to designing usable and useful technical solutions for and with future users, enabling them to avoid involuntary non-use. PD widens the focus of the design process to include the use practices that the future solution will be part of and engages future users in designing their own technological future. The paper reports on seven of our own PD projects to show that PD can yield alternative technical solutions aligned with the logic of users’ activities and appropriate to their capabilities. PD aims at the design of technologies that enhance its users’ autonomy, and our research shows that the design of the interaction – the user interface and interaction mechanisms – is key for enabling use and avoiding involuntary non-use.

W7214951707.t: Jokaisenoikeudet—meaning “every person’s right’’ in Finnish—refers to the ancient right of public access to natural spaces enshrined in law across Nordic and Baltic countries. This workshop draws on Jokaisenoikeudet as a conceptual lens to reimagine the relationships between humans, nature, and technology in the context of AI design. Specifically, we engage with questions of sustainable AI deployment in natural environments, citizen ownership of and access to AI systems, and the transparency and governance of data collected in these contexts. The workshop is grounded in a transdisciplinary collaboration between Arizona State University, Tampere University, and the University of Helsinki, centered on the participatory design of a modular EdgeAI device for natural environments—and, crucially, on the collective curation of the datasets that will shape it. Participants will engage in a structured series of gamified co-design activities—including future scenarios, narratives, and storyboards—to interrogate these questions and produce speculative design artefacts. To orient this inquiry toward constructive futures, the workshop draws on Solarpunk: a literary, artistic, and social movement envisioning worlds in which humanity, technology, and nature coexist in harmony. Positioned at the intersection of speculative and participatory design, ecological thinking, and HCI research, this workshop contributes to a growing discourse on the social and environmental responsibilities of AI design—and invites the NordiCHI community to help shape it.
